title: How to use AI to create and update SOPs
summary: How to use AI to draft an SOP from a screen recording — and, more importantly, how to keep it current once the process it documents starts changing.
body_markdown:
> Our navigation menu changed, so I had to update every single onboarding video with the new navigation.


That is an operations lead describing most of her quarter. The process she had documented hadn't changed at all. Same steps, same order, same outcome. A menu moved, and every screenshot in her SOP library pointed at something that was no longer there.


Teams buy AI to solve the blank page, because the blank page is the part everyone can see. Someone knows the task cold and nobody has an afternoon to write it down. That cost is real, and AI removes most of it. The cost nobody budgets for arrives eighteen months later, when forty procedures all quietly stop matching the software they describe.


## What is an AI-generated SOP?


An AI-generated SOP is a standard operating procedure drafted from a recording of the task rather than written from scratch. The tool detects each step, writes the instruction for it, and attaches the screenshot that matches. A person then edits for accuracy, which is a meaningfully different job from authoring.


The distinction that matters is where the draft comes from. A generator working off a written prompt ("write an SOP for offboarding a contractor") produces plausible prose about a process it has never seen. You then check every line against your actual system, which is most of the work you were trying to avoid. A generator working off a screen recording produces steps that mirror what happened on screen, so the editing pass is correction rather than verification.


## How do you turn a screen recording into an SOP?


Even a rough screen recording is a great resource that can be turned into an SOP. Here’s how you do it:


1. **Pick one procedure with one end state.** "Process a refund" is a procedure. "Manage billing" is a department. Our guide to[creating SOP templates](https://www.clueso.io/blog/create-sop-templates) is a reasonable scaffold for deciding where one document should stop.
2. **Do the task once, narrating as you go.** Your narration becomes the draft instructions and your screen becomes the screenshots. Do the task properly rather than performing it.
3. **Generate the draft.**[Clueso](https://www.clueso.io/tools/sop-generator) takes that single[screen recording](https://www.clueso.io/features/screen-recorder) and produces a formatted[step-by-step guide](https://www.clueso.io/features/help-articles) with screenshots alongside a narrated video, so the written procedure and the walkthrough come out of the same capture instead of being built twice.
4. **Edit for accuracy, then cut.** Proofread your SOP once and fix if there are any errors.
5. **Publish where the work happens.** An SOP in a folder nobody opens is a document, not a procedure.

## Why do SOPs go out of date faster than teams plan for?


Creating SOPs without any tools is an intensive and slow task. Given how fast products change how they look and work, it’s easy for an SOP to go out of date.


Usually, three things break an SOP. There’s either a process change or the product itself has new fields or screens that a user needs to navigate. A new regulation changes one step in the middle of a sequence that is otherwise fine. In every case the procedure is 90% correct, which is worse than being wrong, because nobody notices until someone follows it and gets stuck.


Static formats make this worse by construction. A procedure built in slides and screenshot tools has no relationship between the document and the system it describes, so a change costs a full re-read to find the three places it appears.


We've written separately about[replacing PowerPoint SOPs with interactive video](https://www.clueso.io/blog/replacing-powerpoint-sops-with-interactive-video) , and about what happens to[SOPs and job aids during a systems migration](https://www.clueso.io/blog/sop-and-job-aid-for-system-change) , when every procedure goes stale on the same day.


## How do you update an SOP when the process changes?


The instinct is to open the document and retype the changed step. That works when there are a few SOPs to manage but it may not survive a whole quarter. That’s because the written procedure and the video walkthrough drift apart. You fix the doc, the video still shows the old menu, and now you have two artifacts disagreeing with each other in front of a new hire.


The better mechanic is to re-record the flow that changed and regenerate from it. Clueso takes the new recording's steps for an existing guide and rewrites both the written article and the video narration together, saving it as a new version rather than requiring a full re-record from scratch.


Two habits make that mechanic pay off. Keep procedures scoped small, because a tight document means a change touches one file rather than four. And record the flow rather than describing it, since a re-recording regenerates a procedure while a written description of what changed does not.


Another factor to keep in mind is translation. Most teams forget that. A change to one English procedure is a change to every language you publish it in, which is why[keeping translations in sync](https://www.clueso.io/features/auto-translate) from the source recording matters more than the initial translation ever did. The same logic applies to the[AI voiceover](https://www.clueso.io/features/ai-voiceovers) on the video, which regenerates from the updated transcript instead of needing the original narrator back.


## What should a human still own?


Accuracy and judgement calls are still things humans should own. Being in charge of what to leave out, which steps carry risk, and when a procedure should be retired instead of updated are all things that you shouldn’t completely automate.


A model will faithfully document a workaround your team invented two years ago for a bug that was fixed last spring. It has no way to know the step is obsolete. Reviewing an SOP is partly checking that it is right and partly asking whether the process it describes should still exist.


## What should you look for in a tool that has to keep SOPs current?


Most evaluations test creation, because creation is what a demo shows. Test the second update instead — change something, regenerate, and see what breaks.


Four questions worth asking a vendor:


- **Does it generate from a real recording, or from a prompt?** This decides whether your editing pass is correction or verification.
- **Does one capture produce both the written procedure and the video?** If they're built separately, they will drift separately.
- **What does updating cost — a re-record, or a regeneration?** Ask to see it done on a document that already exists.
- **Do updates carry through to every language and every embedded location?** A procedure that updates in English and stays stale in German has a maintenance problem wearing a different hat.

If the same question applies to your help center rather than your internal procedures, we've covered[keeping help center articles current](https://www.clueso.io/blog/how-to-automatically-update-help-center-articles) and[keeping a training video library from going stale](https://www.clueso.io/blog/training-video-library) separately. Teams standardizing across regions usually end up templating the output, which is what[Clueprints](https://www.clueso.io/clueprints) are for.


## Where to start


Open the three procedures your team re-explains most and check when each was last touched against when that software last shipped a UI change. If the gap is more than a couple of releases, record one of those flows again this week and regenerate it. You'll find out in ten minutes whether updating costs you a regeneration or a rewrite, which is the number that decides how big a library you can afford to run.


## Frequently asked questions


**Which tools auto-generate SOPs from screen recordings?**


You can use Clueso to capture your screen and detect steps that should be part of an SOP automatically. The output will include both the written steps and the matching screenshots from your actual system.


**Can AI write an SOP?**


AI can draft one, and the draft is usable when it's generated from a recording of the real task. A person still reviews it for accuracy and decides which steps matter. AI removes the authoring effort, not the judgment.


**How do you automate SOP creation without losing accuracy?**


Generate from a screen recording rather than a text prompt, keep each procedure scoped to one task, and treat the output as a draft to correct rather than a document to approve. Accuracy comes from the capture being real.


**Can documentation update automatically when workflows change?**


Partly. Regenerating a procedure from a new recording is solved and takes minutes. Detecting that a process changed in the first place is still a human trigger in most tools, which is why a review cadence matters more than teams expect.


**How do you keep a written SOP and its training video in sync?**


Generate both from the same recording, and regenerate both from the same re-recording. Maintaining them as separate artifacts is what causes a document and a video to contradict each other.
